title: NeurIPS 2025 Test of Time 颁奖演讲：目标检测简史（节选）
speaker: 何恺明 Kaiming He
desc: "Faster R-CNN" 获 NeurIPS 2025 时间考验奖（Test of Time Award），唯一到场的合著者何恺明代四位作者登台，以《目标检测简史》为题回望技术演进：从 1996 年他读过的第一篇计算机视觉论文（用神经网络做人脸检测），到 SIFT、HOG、DPM 手工特征时代的巅峰，直至深度学习复兴前夜。
focus: 跟读学者开场与学术叙事语流：Kaiming He 清晰沉稳的口语（语速适中易跟读），"Welcome to the talk, everyone" 开场与自我介绍句式，"test of time"、"object detection"、"bounding box"、"handcrafted" 等计算机视觉高频术语，以及 "Surprisingly…" 排比叙事节奏。

sentences.text: Welcome to the talk, everyone.
My name is Kaiming He, and I'm doing this presentation on behalf of my dear friends and co-authors.
Shaoqing Ren, Ross Girshick, and Jian Sun.
I'm doing this presentation just partially because I'm the only person who can make it here.
Okay, so this is the title of today's presentation, A Brief History of Visual Object Detection.
So why I decided to take this title?
Because I feel it is difficult to talk about a work that is 10 years ago.
I need to set up a context correctly. And then when I started to think about the context, I need to talk about the context of the context and so forth, so and so forth.
And then I decided to talk about the history of object detection, not just the paper in itself.
Let's see how it goes.
So first of all, what is object detection?
Or what is object detection in computer vision?
So conceptually, it's a very simple task for human beings.
But it has been very challenging in computer vision for many decades.
So the task is about recognizing the objects and localizing them simultaneously.
So usually, their localization is represented by a bounding box.
And the recognition is represented by some confidence of a class category.
So it's difficult to talk about history while we need to stop somewhere.
So I decided to set the stop sign 30 years ago.
So I will start from this paper.
Interestingly, this is the first computer vision paper I have ever read.
Surprisingly, this paper was published in CVPR 1996.
Surprisingly, this paper used neural networks, which is not popular at that time.
And also surprisingly, it looks like it works pretty good.
And again, surprisingly, it won a test of time award ten years after that.
So I read this paper in 2007 when I was an undergrad.
I spent my entire semester trying to reproduce it.
Then I got stuck because I realized that I spent the entire summer just reproducing how backpropagation was done with the tanh activation function.
I just want to give you some idea of how difficult things were at that time.
Interestingly, even though that paper has some promising signal of using neural networks at that time, the community of computer vision deviates from the direction of using neural networks.
So surprisingly, at that time, some other methods are more popular.
For example, just one year after the previous paper.
People started to use support vector machines or SVM for the same face detection task.
Well, at that time, support vector machines are very popular.
They are kind of the most powerful machine learning tools that we can use in computer vision.
Interestingly, this paper won another test-of-time award 10 years later.
Then the computer vision community started to look at their hand-engineering features for the usage of any machine learning classifier, such as an SVM or a boosting classifier.
At that time, one of the most successful framework is called the Viola Jones algorithm.
And in today's world, this is kind of a convolutional kernel with handcrafted weights.
The weights are very simple. Half of them are black and the other half of them are white.
The kernels may have different resolutions and so on and so forth.
While this feature looks very simple, it turns out that this method works very well in computer vision.
It has been kind of a golden baseline for many years in face detection and many other tasks.
Then the computer vision, at almost the same time, started to look deeper into the design of handcrafted features.
And these are two of the most successful and most widely used features in the vision community.
So on the left, it is SIFT, which is short for Scale Invariant Feature Transform.
And on the right, it is HOG, which is short for Histogram of Gradients.
Conceptually, these two features are kind of orientation gradients.
They would be slightly higher level than some other features at that time, such as Edges or their Viola Jones features.
So very quickly in computer vision, these features became very popular and very powerful.
Then people start to build more powerful classifier on top of these features.
And surprisingly, some of the simplest classifier works the best.
So this is a work from 2003.
Interestingly, the paper title is called Video Google.
But conceptually, the core idea is actually a bag of words, or bag of visual words.
So in today's terminology, you can understand this as kind of global pooling or average pooling.
That's what our community can do at that time.
Then people started to get a little bit further after that.
So instead of using a global or a very large pooling window.
People started to look at something that is called pyramids in computer vision, which is kind of multi-scale representation.
So there are two very related and very powerful methods published at that time.
So one is called Pyramid Match Kernel, and the other is called Spatial Pyramid Matching.
Interestingly, these works all won some Test of Time awards 10 years after they were published.
And then the visual community started to build some higher-level, slightly higher-level representations than these handcrafted representations.
So one of the most powerful methods at that time is called Deformable Parts Models or DPM in short.
